title: Cauda equina syndrome
subtitle: Suspect early, scan the same day, decompress

sources.org: Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), NHS England
sources.title: National suspected cauda equina syndrome (CES) pathway

sources.org: Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS) and British Association of Spine Surgeons (BASS)
sources.title: Standards of care for investigation and management of cauda equina syndrome

sources.org: Todd NV, British Journal of Neurosurgery
sources.title: Guidelines for cauda equina syndrome. Red flags and white flags. Systematic review and implications for triage (Br J Neurosurg 2017;31:336-339)

red_flags.text: New urinary disturbance with back pain or sciatica: reduced bladder sensation, hesitancy, poor stream, loss of the desire to void, or retention.
Altered sensation in the saddle area, perineum or genitals, including on wiping after the toilet.
Bilateral sciatica, or sciatica that alternates sides.
New sexual dysfunction or new bowel disturbance, including incontinence or loss of rectal sensation.
Painless retention with overflow: this is late, and outcomes are worse than when the bladder still has sensation.

do_now.text: Treat suspected CES as a surgical emergency at any hour. Do not wait for daylight or for the symptoms to progress.
Arrange emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine, following the time standard in the national pathway.
Bladder scan for post-void residual volume, and catheterise if in retention.
Contact the on-call spinal surgeon as soon as MRI confirms compression, so theatre can be planned without delay.

assess.text: Document the time of onset of each symptom, especially bladder symptoms. This defines the clinical category and later decisions.
Full lower-limb neurological examination, including saddle and perianal sensation to light touch and pin prick, recorded by dermatome.
Perianal sensation and anal tone, with a chaperone and with consent; record what was examined and what was found.
Classify as suspected, incomplete (CES-I, altered bladder sensation but preserved control) or with retention (CES-R).

investigate.text: MRI lumbosacral spine. If MRI is contraindicated, CT myelography per local protocol.
Post-void residual volume by bladder scan, interpreted alongside symptoms rather than as a single cut-off.
Coagulation screen and group and save before theatre.
Consider other causes when MRI does not show compression: conus lesions, tumour, infection, and haematoma.

resuscitate.text: Analgesia is adequate and does not mask the diagnosis. Repeat the neurological and bladder assessment after it.
Stop or reverse anticoagulants in preparation for surgery, per local protocol.

definitive.text: Surgical decompression as soon as possible after radiological confirmation, by the most appropriately experienced surgeon available.
Decompression of a central disc prolapse is by discectomy, with laminectomy if needed for safe access to the thecal sac.
If MRI does not show compression, give written safety-net advice listing the red flags and how to return.

escalate.text: If no MRI is available locally, transfer the same day to a unit with MRI and spinal surgery. Do not admit to wait for the morning list.
Communicate the MRI result to the patient promptly, including a normal result with safety-netting.
Arrange urology, pelvic floor and psychological follow-up for persisting bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.

notes: Cauda equina syndrome is a clinical diagnosis with a radiological confirmation. Most suspected cases have normal scans, and that is the correct cost of not missing one.
Retention is a late sign. The patient to catch is the one with altered bladder sensation and preserved control.
Document negatives: saddle sensation, bladder function and anal tone, with the time. This protects the patient and you.
